title: Force as the last resort
hook: peace first; force only when every other means has failed

segments.voice: Yesterday, women in the teaching: why call her bad, from whom kings are born? Your line was equals. Whose voice did you make room for? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

A letter, written in Persian verse, sent to an emperor. The man who wrote it had lost his father to that empire's executioner, and had lost his sons too. He had every reason to write in pure rage. Instead the letter does something slower. It reminds the emperor of oaths he swore and broke. It talks about God, and about what a ruler owes the people. And somewhere in the middle comes one line that Sikhs still carry, a line about when a sword may be lifted at all. The letter is the Zafarnama, from Guru Gobind Singh. The line is today's lesson.
screen: `A LETTER IN PERSIAN VERSE.` → `TO AN EMPEROR WHO BROKE HIS OATHS.` → `ONE LINE ABOUT THE SWORD.`

segments.voice: First, the line itself. In paraphrase, the Zafarnama says: when every other means has been tried and has failed, then it is right to take the sword in hand. Notice the order. The sword is not the first word. It is what's left when the other words have run out. Second, what comes before it. A good deal comes before it. Talking. Bargaining. Promises taken in good faith. Patience. Tradition says the Guru's side had trusted sworn oaths before they were broken. The letter isn't a war cry; it's a reckoning, and its first weapon is the truth said plainly to power. Third, a picture of the person who holds the sword. A salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the Guru's father, near the very end of the Granth, says it in paraphrase: the one who frightens no one, and is frightened of no one, is the wise one. Both halves matter. Not frightened: the courage to stand. Frightening no one: no taste for bullying, no swagger. Initiated Sikhs carry the kirpan, the small sword, as a sign of that pairing. Sikhs explain it as a duty to protect, not a license to threaten. Fourth, an ordinary Tuesday. Most days, nobody reaches for a sword. But the order still applies to a raised voice, a cutting email, a door slammed. Peace first. Talk first. Truth first, plainly said. And only when every other way has truly been tried does anything harder come out. The hard part is honesty about the word every. It's easy to say you tried everything after trying one thing twice.
screen: `ZAFARNAMA: ONLY WHEN ALL ELSE FAILS.` · `FIRST: WORDS, PATIENCE, TRUTH.` · `FRIGHTEN NONE, FEAR NONE.` · `THE ORDER ON AN ORDINARY DAY.` · then, large: `PEACE FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: seek one peaceful way. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one conflict that's live for you right now, big or small. Notice what part of you wants to swing first. Then, breath by breath, list the gentler ways still untried: a calmer conversation, a question instead of a charge, a letter rather than a shout, a third person to help. Choose one. Hold it in mind as the next step. The bell holds the time.
Force as the last resort. The Zafarnama's teaching that the sword is lifted only when every other means has failed; frighten no one, fear no one. Today's word.
screen: `FORCE AS THE LAST RESORT — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: peace first. Today, before any sharp reply, ask yourself one question: have I really tried every gentler way? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-four.

notes: The Zafarnama verse is paraphrased; please confirm wording and that it is addressed to Aurangzeb (the script does not name him).
The hook says the writer had lost his father to the empire's executioner and his sons to its wars; please confirm this framing is acceptable as background.
'Tradition says the Guru's side had trusted sworn oaths before they were broken' refers to the oaths at Anandpur; please check.
Please confirm Ang 1427 for Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok 'bhai kahu ko det neh, neh bhai manat an'.
